lesson.title: Transition State: The Peak of the Reaction Coordinate
lesson.summary: Clarifies that transition state and activated complex describe the same high-energy peak, and draws the important distinction between a transition state and a genuine reaction intermediate.
lesson.body:
In most general and AP-level chemistry treatments, "transition state" and "activated complex" describe the exact same thing: the transient, high energy species sitting at the very top of the activation energy barrier, discussed in the previous two sections. Where a slight difference in emphasis is sometimes drawn, "activated complex" tends to describe the actual chemical structure at that moment, which atoms and which bonds are partially broken and partially formed, while "transition state" tends to describe the single point on the energy diagram itself, the exact peak along the reaction coordinate, sometimes described more formally as a maximum in energy along the reaction pathway. For the purposes of this course, treat the two terms as interchangeable unless a question specifically asks you to distinguish them.

One distinction genuinely does matter, and it is commonly confused: a transition state, sitting at a peak, is not the same thing as a reaction intermediate, which sits in a valley. An intermediate is a real, if often short lived and hard to isolate, chemical species with its own genuine energy minimum, meaning it occupies a dip on the energy diagram and could, in principle, be detected, trapped, or even isolated under the right experimental conditions. A transition state, by contrast, sits at a peak, has no energy minimum at all, and by definition cannot be isolated under any conditions whatsoever, because it exists for only a single instant of atomic rearrangement before immediately sliding back down toward either reactants or products.

Worked example, a two-step reaction energy diagram that makes both a transition state and a genuine intermediate visible on the same picture (kept brief here, since the full detail of multi-step mechanisms belongs elsewhere in the curriculum):

Reactants: 0 kJ/mol
First transition state (TS1): 90 kJ/mol
Intermediate: 30 kJ/mol
Second transition state (TS2): 70 kJ/mol
Products: -20 kJ/mol

Two separate transition states appear in this diagram, one for each of the two steps, with a genuine intermediate sitting in the valley between them, at 30 kJ/mol, well above the reactants but still a real energy minimum rather than a peak. Step 1 has activation energy Ea1 = 90 - 0 = 90 kJ/mol. Step 2 has activation energy Ea2 = 70 - 30 = 40 kJ/mol. Because step 1's barrier, 90 kJ/mol, is higher than step 2's barrier, 40 kJ/mol, step 1 is the slower of the two steps, and in a multi-step reaction it is the slowest step that limits how fast the overall reaction can proceed.

Every transition state, regardless of how many steps a mechanism has, obeys the same rules already covered in this unit: an unstable, peak-energy configuration that requires both the correct amount of energy and, as the final section of this unit makes explicit, the correct collision orientation to be reached in the first place.
